title: A held-out validation protocol for shape-generalization claims in kernel dispatch, with positive and negative evidence on GB10
abstract: Dispatch rules for GPU kernels - which variant runs at which input shape, and when to trust it - are claims about shape space, and validating them on the shapes they were tuned on is circular. We present a held-out validation protocol for such claims, stated as five requirements: the rule and any admission filter are frozen before test shapes exist; test shapes are fresh, disjoint samples from the benchmark's own generators; comparators, including budgeted autotuning and torch.compile, are charged honestly for probe and compilation costs, with delivery and total regret reported separately; statistics are paired per shape with sample sizes; and every claim ships in a structured record. Applied on a DGX Spark (GB10, sm_120) over reduction, conv-as-gemm and layer-normalization families, the protocol yields three positive results and one negative with mechanism. A zero-probe family-local gate beats every cold-start budgeted autotune on total time including probes; autotuning pays only after roughly 15-260 revisits per shape. At one-shot deployment no arm dominates: torch.compile ties the gate on reduction-like work and loses decisively on conv-as-gemm, replicated across days, so the honest policy is hybrid. Elementwise latency collapses in (bytes per thread, resident waves) to 0.55 percent median residual, against 36 percent for bytes per thread alone. Finally, a trained admission guard transfers rank-ordering across op families (AUC 0.99) but not its calibrated operating point (precision 0.17 against a 0.90 target); the failure localizes to family-constant features, so calibration is bind-time family-local. Scripts, frozen rules, preregistrations and all result files are released; single-accelerator scope is stated explicitly.
